articles.title: In 1998, an Australian couple spent 11 years turning a forgotten 30-acre rainforest into a glow-worm attraction without cutting a tree
articles.summary: In 1998, Ian and Jennifer Moore stumbled upon a colony of glow-worms on an overlooked 30-acre stretch of rainforest on Tamborine Mountain, Queensland.
articles.body: In 1998, Ian and Jennifer Moore stumbled upon a colony of glow-worms on an overlooked 30-acre stretch of rainforest on Tamborine Mountain, Queensland. The discovery gave them an idea that would eventually take years to realise. They began with night-time tours in 1999 before planning a raised walkway and steel bridge through the forest. After nearly five years of planning and construction, the Tamborine Rainforest Skywalk opened in 2009. The Moores said the elevated attraction was built without cutting down any forest trees, turning a once-inaccessible part of their property into a destination for visitors.How Ian and Jennifer Moore built a rainforest retreat from a 130-acre propertyIan and Jennifer Moore returned to Queensland after spending 17 years in Perth, Western Australia, an official Tamborine Rainforest Skywalk reported. They wanted a business that would give them a different way of life, and in 1988 they purchased 130 acres of land on Tamborine Mountain. The property had a small house and established gardens, while Tamborine Mountain Road ran through the middle of the estate.The couple converted the house into a restaurant, opening Songbirds in the Forest in 1989. Its outdoor dining setting, surrounded by gardens, attracted visitors from the Gold Coast and beyond, including people travelling from interstate and overseas. As the business grew, they added six accommodation studios and developed Songbirds Rainforest Retreat.The land below the road followed a different course. Its 30 acres had no known access, and with the restaurant and accommodation taking up their attention, the area remained largely unexplored by the owners. That changed one night in 1998.Old timber tracks helped turn the hidden forest into a visitor attractionDuring a visit to the lower property, the Moores discovered a large colony of glow-worms beside Cedar Creek. The site suggested that the forest could become part of a visitor experience in its own right, rather than remaining an inaccessible section of the estate.The first idea was relatively modest. They planned night-time eco-tours that would allow visitors to see the glow-worms in their natural surroundings. Before those trips could begin, however, they needed a way to reach the site.Their search for access led to an unexpected piece of local history. Timber workers had already established tracks through the area in the early 20th century, when they harvested red cedar, rose gum and crow’s ash. The old routes had become overgrown, but clearing the invasive lantana made it possible to adapt them for use by minibuses.The glow-worm tours began in 1999 and continued nightly until 2004. They brought people into a part of the property that had rarely been visited, even as the forest itself remained the main attraction.The Moores sold Songbirds to focus on their new rainforest attractionFor several years, visitors experienced the area after dark. The tours also gave the Moores a closer understanding of what the property could offer during daylight hours, when the rainforest, its rock pools and the surrounding vegetation could be seen in greater detail.They began considering a structure that would allow people to move through the forest at an elevated level. The plan developed into a raised walkway and high steel bridge, with a central building intended to provide information about the surrounding environment.By 2004, the couple had decided to commit to the new venture. They sold the remaining Songbirds property and turned their attention to creating the attraction that would become the Tamborine Rainforest Skywalk.How the family built an elevated walkway above the rainforest floorThe project required almost five years of planning, research and approvals from state authorities and the local council. The site presented practical difficulties, including steep volcanic soils and the challenge of installing large steel structures within an established rainforest.The construction relied on heavy lifting equipment rather than clearing a broad route through the trees. Cranes weighing up to 120 tonnes, with booms reaching 80 metres, were used to position the bridge towers and the walkway sections. Some of the components measured 40 metres long and had to be carefully manoeuvred over the canopy before being lowered into place.The central building was delivered in sections and assembled on-site. The work demanded careful positioning because the structure had to be installed above the forest floor while leaving the surrounding vegetation intact.The Moores' stated achievement was that no forest trees were cut down during the installation of the Skywalk. Their sons, Brendan and Nicholas, joined the project during this period, contributing their experience in marketing and ecotourism. The development became a family undertaking, with different members bringing their own knowledge to the planning and construction process.The rainforest needed attention beyond constructionThe Moores' plans extended beyond building a bridge and opening the site to visitors. They also established ongoing work to maintain the property's vegetation, including planting native species and removing invasive plants.The Richmond birdwing butterfly became another focus. The species faces conservation pressures, and the property has a programme intended to provide suitable habitat. The family has also worked to maintain a butterfly colony through breeding efforts involving other Australian colonies, seeking to reduce the risks associated with a small, isolated population.These efforts formed part of the longer-term management of the site. The attraction depended on the rainforest remaining a living environment, rather than simply providing a backdrop for the elevated walkway.Opening the Skywalk in 2009The Tamborine Rainforest Skywalk officially opened in 2009, with then federal tourism minister Martin Ferguson attending the ceremony. By that point, the project had taken more than a decade to progress from the original glow-worm discovery to a purpose-built rainforest attraction.The site offered visitors a different way to experience the landscape, with elevated paths and a bridge taking them above the forest floor. Its origins, however, remained tied to the creek where the Moores had found the glow-worms and the tours that first brought visitors into the neglected section of their property.The Skywalk is now managed by Brendan and Nicholas Moore. The family's involvement has continued beyond the opening, with the attraction operating as a tourism business while maintaining its focus on the surrounding rainforest.You use AI every day. articles.title: “Maze is glass, somehow I’m lost”: Bermondsey schoolgirl wins national writing contest with six words, beating nearly 950 young writers
articles.summary: A schoolgirl from Bermondsey has won a national competition that asked young writers to tell a story in just six words.
articles.body: A schoolgirl from Bermondsey has won a national competition that asked young writers to tell a story in just six words. Amal Badmus, a Year 10 student at St Saviour’s and St Olave’s Church of England School, was selected from nearly 950 young writers from 26 schools.Her winning story, “Maze is glass, somehow I’m lost.” impressed the judging panel at Penguin Random House.According to the Southwark News, the competition is inspired by Ernest Hemingway’s famous six-word story, “For sale: baby shoes, never worn”, and encourages students to express their ideas through short pieces of writing. Amal’s entry was praised for its impact and relevance to younger readers, while her school’s head teacher congratulated her on the achievement.Amal Badmus wins 2026 six-word story competition with six-word entryAmal Badmus was crowned the winner of the national 2026 Six Word Story competition after her entry impressed the Penguin Random House judging panel. The Year 10 student from St Saviour’s and St Olave’s Church of England School was selected from nearly 950 young writers representing 26 different schools.Her winning entry read, “Maze is glass, somehow I’m lost.” The short piece received praise for conveying meaning in just six words. The competition challenges students to explore their storytelling abilities and develop their own unique voices through creative writing.Amal’s success placed her ahead of hundreds of other young participants in a national competition designed to test how effectively young writers can communicate ideas with very few words.Six-word story competition challenges students to make every word countThe Six Word Story competition takes inspiration from author Ernest Hemingway’s famous six-word story, “For sale: baby shoes, never worn”. The format challenges writers to create a story using only six words, making every word important to the meaning of the finished piece.The competition encourages students across the country to discover their own unique voices and develop their storytelling abilities. Rather than relying on lengthy descriptions, participants must convey meaning within a strict word limit.Amal’s winning entry, “Maze is glass, somehow I’m lost,” was praised by the judges for the impact it achieved in such a short space. Her success demonstrated the kind of concise storytelling the competition aims to encourage among young writers.Why did Amal Badmus’s six-word story impress the judgesThe Penguin Random House judging panel praised Amal’s story for its impact and relevance to younger readers. The judges said the piece would particularly resonate with young people facing challenges that could affect their futures in unknown ways.Explaining their decision, the panel said: “This short story is our winner because it packs a punch and really made us think - which is so impressive to do with just six words. Well done, Amal!”The judges’ comments highlighted the effect of Amal’s entry despite its brevity. Her story was selected from nearly 950 young writers across 26 schools, making her the national competition’s winner for 2026.How did Amal’s six-word story earn praise from her head teacherCatherine May, head teacher at St Saviour’s and St Olave’s Church of England School, said, “I was absolutely thrilled when I heard that Amal had won this competition”“It’s a great challenge to convey meaning in so few words, and I’m incredibly impressed with the skill and talent shown here. We are very proud of Amal and her powerful piece of writing…”National finalists in the competition, which is run by creative writing charity First Story, received a book bundle from Penguin Random House, printed postcards of their story, a notebook and a certificate.You use AI every day. articles.title: US government bans Chinese AI company DeepSeek that had wiped more than $1 trillion from Wall Street in less than 2 hours, from all civilian agency IT systems
articles.summary: The US Homeland Security Department has ordered the removal of products and third-party services of Chinese AI company Deepseek.
articles.body: The US Homeland Security Department has ordered the removal of products and third-party services of Chinese AI company Deepseek. In an order, DHS has banned US civilian agency IT systems from using any DeepSeek AI model. The US government is also banning acquisition of products and third-party services developed using DeepSeek technology by US civilian government agencies. In an order, DHS said that DeepSeek models pose "multiple threat vectors" and raised concerns that use of the product "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by US government employees ⁠or vendors." In its order, DHS also said that the use of DeepSeek by government agencies "could produce actionable intelligence on US persons and/or government agencies. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities."In a memo passed in July this year, DHS told federal agencies to monitor flows of traffic in and out of government websites to address potential risks from DeepSeek. Previously, ​several US agencies, including the Department of Commerce and the Navy, have banned ​the use of DeepSeek on government devices. Multiple states including New York, Tennessee, and Virginia have ‌taken ⁠similar steps.When DeepSeek wiped hundreds of billions from WallStreet in one dayIncidentally, DeepSeek is the same Chinese AI company whose low-cost artificial intelligence (AI) model sent shock waves in the US stock market in January 2025. The selloff in the US stock market was prompted by the release of the free AI assistant from China's DeepSeek that the startup said needed less data at a fraction of the cost of services from American technology companies.DeepSeek worries wiped over a trillion dollars from market value of some of the biggest US companies in semiconductor, power and infrastructure sectors. Nvidia alone lost about 17% or close to $593 billion in market value, a record one-day loss for any company.What the summary of the DHS order on DeepSeek saysThe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is publishing notice of the Secretary of Homeland Security’s issuance of an order (1) excluding information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co, Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in applicable regulations, from federal civilian agency procurements; and, (2) removing all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology.FCC to ban Chinese labs from testing US gadgets and equipmentEarlier this month, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said that it will vote on October 29 to bar all Chinese labs from testing electronic devices such as smartphones, cameras and computers for use ‌in the US, widening a previous action targeting Beijing. The FCC said it will prohibit test labs and certification bodies in countries including China that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based test labs. In ⁠2025, the FCC banned testing of US electronics by labs owned or controlled by the Chinese government, and several dozen labs were barred.FCC Chair Brendan Carr had then said that 82% of electronics were tested in China, which does not have an agreement with ​the US. But the agency said this year that a substantial majority of China-based test labs were still ​testing US electronics. "Less than 4% of all electronic devices are tested in labs located inside the US," Carr said, adding the FCC will "insist on fair and reciprocal treatment in international commerce."You use AI every day. articles.title: Rubio India visit: Bilateral with Jaishankar, Jamnagar refinery tour & trade deal - whats on agenda
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will begin a three-day visit to India on Tuesday, with talks on a proposed bilateral trade deal, energy security and
articles.body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will begin a three-day visit to India on Tuesday, with talks on a proposed bilateral trade deal, energy security and strategic cooperation expected to feature prominently during his meetings with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and other engagements in Mumbai and Gujarat’s Jamnagar.Rubio is scheduled to arrive at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport at 2.15 pm on Tuesday, according to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). He will lay a wreath at the Taj memorial to honour the victims of the 26/11 terror attacks before holding bilateral talks with Jaishankar at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel.The two leaders are expected to discuss the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, including energy, trade and investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and the situation in West Asia. Rubio will later attend the “Freedom 250 Reception” at the Jio World Convention Centre to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence. Jaishankar will be the guest of honour.Trade deal and energy security in focusThe visit comes as both countries seek to advance negotiations on a proposed trade agreement amid friction over tariffs, energy imports and immigration policies.Speaking in Uzbekistan ahead of his India visit, Rubio said the two sides were close to finalising the agreement."We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that."Rubio also linked the negotiations to Washington’s decision to grant a temporary waiver on certain sanctions related to Russian energy purchases. He said India’s energy requirements and its importance as a US partner were among the factors being considered."These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.He added that India had diversified its energy sources but continued to rely on Russian supplies because shifting to alternatives could not happen overnight."You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added.India and the US have been negotiating the proposed trade pact since early 2025, seeking to address tariff disputes, reduce non-tariff barriers and improve market access. Jaishankar recently said the negotiations were nearing a "landing point".Jamnagar visit and meeting with AmbaniRubio will travel to Jamnagar in Gujarat on Wednesday, where he is expected to visit Reliance Industries’ oil refining complex and meet chairman Mukesh Ambani before returning to Mumbai. The Jamnagar leg of the visit is expected to last around nine hours.The visit comes as Reliance Industries prepares for a planned investment in a Texas oil refinery, bringing energy cooperation and private-sector investment into focus. Officials have not confirmed reports that Rubio may also visit the Vantara animal rehabilitation centre in Jamnagar.Rubio is also expected to engage with Indian business leaders during his visit, although meetings with industrialists Gautam Adani and Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran have not been officially confirmed.Visit comes amid strains in bilateral tiesRubio’s trip is his second visit to India this year, following his May visit, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Jaishankar and attended a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting.Bilateral relations have faced strains following US tariffs on Indian goods, disagreements over Washington’s claims about its role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military conflict in May 2025, and changes to US immigration policies, including higher H-1B visa fees.The two sides are also expected to exchange views on the West Asia crisis and regional stability. Rubio’s visit follows his meetings with Central Asian foreign ministers in Uzbekistan, where he promoted US trade, security and investment ties with the region.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Maryland landowners refused access to their properties for a 67-mile power-line project; appeals court upholds order allowing surveys before state approval
articles.summary: A US appeals court has upheld an order allowing PSEG Renewable Transmission LLC to access private properties in Maryland to conduct surveys for its
articles.body: A US appeals court has upheld an order allowing PSEG Renewable Transmission LLC to access private properties in Maryland to conduct surveys for its proposed 67-mile Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, despite opposition from landowners and pending state approval. According to the Fourth Circuit, the Arentz Family and 116 other property owners refused access. The project’s application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity remained administratively incomplete because required field studies had not been completed. The court backed survey access before final approval, while the Maryland Public Service Commission’s review of the project remained ongoing.Why Maryland landowners challenged access for a major power-line projectPSEG is developing the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a high-voltage transmission line intended to supply electricity to Maryland and the surrounding region. According to the Fourth Circuit's judgment, the proposed line would extend approximately 67 miles across Baltimore County, Carroll County and Frederick County. The project was selected by PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission organisation, following a 2023 solicitation for proposals to address growing electricity demand and the retirement of power-generation facilities.The dispute involved the Arentz Family and 116 other defendant-appellants who refused to allow PSEG onto their properties. The court record states that the affected land included multi-generational farms, properties subject to forest and wetland conservation easements, and land used for commercial businesses. PSEG sought access to carry out surveys needed to assess the project's environmental and socioeconomic effects and support its application for state approval.Why Maryland flagged PSEG’s power-line applicationMaryland requires a transmission-line developer to obtain a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland Public Service Commission before construction can begin. PSEG submitted its application in December 2024, and the commission referred the question of completeness to the state's Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), part of the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.In March 2025, the PPRP reported that it lacked sufficient information to determine whether the application was complete. PSEG had submitted desktop studies based on secondary sources because it could not access the properties, but the programme said those studies could not be verified and that field studies were necessary. The application was consequently classified as “administratively incomplete”. The court record states that the PPRP estimated it would take approximately 30 months to assess a CPCN application after filing.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Vijayadashami: Victory of awareness over ego
articles.summary: By Swami Sukhabodhananda Every year on Vijayadashami, we celebrate Ram’s victory over Ravan and the Divine Mother’s victory over Mahishasur.
articles.body: By Swami SukhabodhanandaEvery year on Vijayadashami, we celebrate Ram’s victory over Ravan and the Divine Mother’s victory over Mahishasur. Effigies burn, prayers rise and goodness is proclaimed victorious. Yet a question remains: if Ravan was destroyed long ago, why does he still seem so alive within us?Mythology is not only a story about the past. It is also a mirror held before the human mind. Ravan had ten heads. We may have a thousand: anger, jealousy, greed, fear, resentment, pride and the endless demand to be right. Burning an effigy takes a few minutes. Understanding tendencies it represents may take a lifetime. The festival therefore asks us to move beyond spectacle into self-enquiry: ‘what am i feeding in myself each day?’Ravan was learned, accomplished and a devotee of Shiv. Yet his learning did not free him from arrogance. This is an uncomfortable reminder that information is not transformation. We may know scriptures and still be unable to accept a simple criticism.Consider two colleagues. One wins an argument but spends the evening replaying every insult. The other loses the argument, learns something and returns home peaceful. Who has truly won? The world measures victory by applause, status and achievement. Spiritual wisdom asks a different question: after the applause fades, what is the quality of your inner life?Ego is not only the loud declaration, “I am superior.” It can whisper, “Nobody respects me,” or “Why was i not appreciated?” Sometimes it even says, “Look how humble i have become.” Ego changes its costume but keeps the same centre: ‘me and mine.’This is why the battle with Mahishasur is so revealing. The demon changes form repeatedly, just as ego shifts from pride to self-pity, from anger to wounded innocence. Durga represents the awakened Shakti that sees through these disguises. Her victory points not merely to the defeat of a demon, but to the dissolution of ignorance.Durga evokes courage to face what we ordinarily avoid. Lakshmi reminds us of the wealth of gratitude, generosity and harmony. Saraswati awakens discrimination and wisdom. On the tenth day, Vijayadashami, this journey finds its symbolic fulfilment.But what exactly is victory? The first victory is recognising our destructive tendencies. The second is refusing to identify with them. Anger may arise, but must i become anger? Fear may visit, but must i build my home in fear?There is a third, subtler victory. The ego that proudly announces, “I have overcome my ego,” has quietly returned through the back door. Awareness does not need to advertise itself. Like light, it simply reveals what is there. We need not hate our weaknesses; hatred only creates another battle. We can observe them with honesty, learn from them and cease giving them unquestioned authority.Ram symbolises dharm: strength guided by wisdom; action rooted in responsibility and power restrained by values. Ravan reminds us that brilliance without inner mastery can become bondage. The real question is not whether we admire Ram, but whether Ram’s qualities guide our responses when life challenges us.Vijay means victory, Dashami marks the tenth lunar day. Let its meaning extend beyond the calendar. Each time understanding replaces resentment, compassion replaces hostility and humility replaces pride, a little Vijayadashami happens within us.Swamiji will be conducting online workshops; for details contact: +91 95135 60103/+91 99017 77003Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with election fraud in California
articles.summary: Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election-related offences in California, including fraudulent voter registration and
articles.body: Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election-related offences in California, including fraudulent voter registration and voting in the November 2024 US elections, the US Department of Justice said on Monday.The accused Indians have been identified as Amandeep Kaur, 30, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, who lives in Sacramento. It was not immediately clear whether either of them was among the 11 people arrested during early morning raids across California under ‘Operation Protect the Vote’.According to the Justice Department, Shah fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast his ballot the same day. Kaur, who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 election.“All 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or 'green card' holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not US citizens and are not permitted to vote in US elections,” the Justice Department said.The charges include making false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration. Both offences are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison.DOJ links accused to voter registration listActing Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all 28 defendants appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people the Justice Department had provided to California election officials the previous week.“Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,” McCotter told reporters in Los Angeles.The charges come amid an escalating dispute between the Trump administration and California officials over allegations of non-citizen voter registration. The Justice Department has also asked a federal court to prevent California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots returned by people on the list, arguing that votes cast illegally could undermine election integrity.California officials have opposed the demand, saying the federal government has not provided sufficient evidence to establish that those listed are non-citizens. They have also argued that withholding or refusing to count ballots could violate federal and state law and disenfranchise eligible voters.Trump administration steps up election investigationsThe Justice Department has intensified investigations into alleged election-related offences as early voting begins in several states. Before Monday’s announcement, it had charged about 90 people with various forms of election misconduct this year, including 50 accused of voting as non-citizens.The department said on Monday that it had charged 113 non-citizens across 20 states with voting and registration offences over the preceding seven weeks.Election law experts have cautioned that such cases do not establish widespread non-citizen voting. They have also warned that aggressive efforts to scrutinise voter rolls could risk removing eligible voters or undermining public confidence in elections.California officials have questioned the Justice Department’s methodology for identifying the 20,000 people, while the federal government has argued that access to additional voter registration data would help verify their citizenship status.You use AI every day. articles.title: Antennae of a nobody
articles.summary: On a morning after a particularly self-reflective night, I found myself in a Kafkaesque situation.
articles.body: On a morning after a particularly self-reflective night, I found myself in a Kafkaesque situation. A look at the mirror hinted I may have grown a pair of antennae. But when I landed on my two feet, I realised the metamorphosis was not quite so dire as Gregor Samsa’s. Unlike him, I was free to do what I pleased, and as anonymously as I had lived much of my life. Yet, with a sense of alienation and a deep desire to find my kin, I headed towards Jantar Mantar, to explore if I had an affinity with the cockroaches.When I reached Parliament Street, it was so full with policemen and barricades that there was little room for the young protesters. These were lean and muscular guys, drawn from a special inventory. Hoping to slip past, I was approaching a barricade when a cop thrust himself before me. “Are you a cockroach?” In a state of self-doubt, I told him I wasn’t. “Substantiate,” he said. I said that I was neither young nor angry. I had made peace with everything odorous, so that I didn’t have to cover my nose anymore.The answer should have set me free, but it made him smile. He said he had the gift of x-ray vision, just by looking at people he could figure them out completely. “Isn’t that what cops mostly do – decide cases by looking at people?” Unhappy with my reply, he examined me as if under a microscope, and concluded that I did not have a govt job, a govt house, retirement funds, lifelong health cover like CGHS, and membership of elite clubs at discounted rates – “all the qualifications of a disgruntled cockroach.” Then he said conclusively, “Your cover is blown.”I was nearly certain that he could see my antennae, which I thought were hidden. “The only thing that I need now is a confession,” he said.He was right, of course. I was a nobody. I could not get anything done without paying a bribe, or standing in a queue. I neither had authority nor connections. Like most people of my country, I had lived in the back lanes, unprotected, uncared for by the state, always scared of authorities, but somehow managing to survive in the gutters on my own. “I think I am a cockroach,” I said. “I am never wrong,” he rejoiced, reaching for his baton.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Batteries first
articles.summary: Last fiscal, India spent about $135bn on imported oil and gas, at a time global prices were low.
articles.body: Last fiscal, India spent about $135bn on imported oil and gas, at a time global prices were low. This year, the bill will be considerably higher, due to Iran war. Oil and gas is our largest import item, and if we curtail it, defending the rupee will be easier. So, electric vehicles look like the answer. But as TOI reported Monday, they are only adding to the import burden. In the five months from April to Aug – after Iran war started, stoking interest in EVs – India’s battery imports from China increased to almost $3bn. Extrapolating, the full-year bill could touch $7bn.That would be justifiable if battery imports offset hydrocarbon imports, to the same or greater extent. But as an HSBC Global Research report pointed out recently, they don’t always. If you’re talking e-scooters, the kind used by delivery agents, or e-rickshaws, or even electric buses, yes, the battery offsets fuel import costs in 2-3 years. But electric cars take 7-8 years, on average. That’s because most cars are low-milers. They sit in parking lots most of the time. So, the more electric cars you have, the bigger your battery import bill – cars have big batteries – without commensurate savings on the hydrocarbon side. And the irony is that govt is encouraging EV adoption with huge subsidies. In Delhi, India’s biggest vehicle market, an expert panel has recommended complete phase-out of petrol and diesel cars by 2040.Should we give up electrification? No, but we must aggressively push battery manufacturing in India. West Asia is a key supplier of oil and gas, but it’s not had a monopoly for decades. Russia, US, Venezuela, etc, there are plenty of other suppliers. But when it comes to lithium batteries, China’s grip on the market should lead to second thoughts. Where we, as a nation, are aiming for 50GWh battery cell manufacturing capacity, some Chinese factories produce much more individually. There’s no point overcoming one kind of import dependence for another.So far, our battery manufacturing story is uninspiring. Our batteries are still made of imported cells and electronics, and manufacturing capacity this time last year was just 1.4GWh. Global demand for lithium batteries is booming, for not only EVs but also storage systems, data centres, etc. The country must take a leap of faith here, creating the whole battery ecosystem, from research to metal refining and manufacturing. We’ve done it before with petroleum refineries. This, too, is doable.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.
